items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Social Commerce: Examining The Influence of AI-Enabled Recommendations on Consumer Engagement and Purchase Behaviour
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become the infrastructural logic of social commerce, where algorithmic recommenders mediate what consumers see, trust and buy. Yet evidence on how AI-enabled recommendations translate into engagement and purchase behaviour inside socially embedded shopping environments remains fragmented. Drawing on the stimulus–organism–response (S-O-R) framework and integrating trust and privacy-calculus reasoning, this study develops and tests a model linking AI recommendation quality and perceived personalisation to consumer engagement and purchase intention. A structurally calibrated dataset of 420 social commerce users was analysed using standardised OLS regression, bootstrapped mediation with 5,000 resamples and moderated regression. AI recommendation quality (β = .228, p < .001) and trust in AI recommendations (β = .349, p < .001) significantly drove consumer engagement (R² = .344), while engagement was the strongest predictor of purchase intention (β = .383, p < .001; R² = .436). Trust transmitted a significant indirect effect from recommendation quality to purchase intention (β = .196, 95% CI [.147, .251]) and perceived personalisation transmitted a significant indirect effect through engagement (β = .196, 95% CI [.142, .255]); trust also influenced purchase intention indirectly through engagement (β = .216, 95% CI [.159, .281]). Privacy concern did not significantly moderate the personalisation–trust link (ΔR² = .006, p = .075), although the interaction was directionally negative. The findings position trust and engagement as the principal conduits through which algorithmic recommendation creates commercial value, and caution that personalisation alone is insufficient without trust-building.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Classification Algorithms for Leukaemia Diagnosis: A Structured Review of Model Performance and Clinical Readiness
items.abstract: Leukaemia diagnosis and classification increasingly combine morphology with immunophenotypic, cytogenetic and molecular information, while artificial intelligence (AI) offers a potential means of standardising image-based assessment and reducing repetitive workload. This structured review critically examines contemporary AI approaches for leukaemia cell and case classification, with emphasis on dataset scale, unit of analysis, validation design, reported performance and clinical readiness. Peer-reviewed literature was identified through a targeted PubMed-focused search updated on 30 July 2026, with publisher and DOI records used to verify study design, numerical results and bibliographic identity. Representative primary human studies were selected only when the reported task, unit of analysis, testing design and principal performance metrics could be verified from the primary report. The evidence shows substantial technical progress, but the interpretation of apparently high performance changes markedly with the level at which generalisation is tested. Image-wise or closely related internal partitions provide weaker evidence of transportability than patient-level internal testing, while genuinely independent institutional or imaging-platform evaluation provides the most clinically informative test of robustness. Across acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, acute myeloid leukaemia and acute promyelocytic leukaemia applications, patient-level separation, external testing, class-balance reporting, transparent reference standards and multimodal diagnostic integration remain decisive. AI should therefore be considered an adjunct to expert haematopathology rather than a stand-alone substitute for contemporary integrated diagnosis. Multicentre prospective evaluation, rigorous reporting and clinically meaningful human-AI workflow studies are priorities for translation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Automated Analysis and Interpretation of Intravascular Ultrasound in Coronary Artery Disease: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) leads to considerable morbidity and mortality worldwide.Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) is an imaging modality to guide percutaneous coronary intervention; however, it requires time-consuming, expert-dependent manual analysis.Artificial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly used for IVUS analysis, but there is limited evidence on its diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility.This review aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance and clinical usefulness of AI for automated IVUS analysis of coronary arteries.The research protocol was prospectively registered (PROSPERO, CRD420261454806) and followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines for systematic reviews.PubMed/MEDLINE and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from inception through July 23, 2026, and July 26, 2026, respectively, for publications assessing AI, machine learning, or deep learning algorithms for the automated analysis of coronary IVUS, including segmentation of structures, identification of plaque types, and quantitative measurements.Two reviewers independently screened and selected eligible studies and extracted the data.The risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 (Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) and visualized using robvis, and the GRADE approach was used to rate the certainty of evidence.Of the 802 records identified (PubMed, n = 216; Cochrane CENTRAL, n = 586), eight studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in this review.They reported on the performance of convolutional neural networks, U-Net/U-Net++, Efficient-UNet, DeepLabv3+-based models, and gradient boosting in segmenting lumen, vessel, plaque, and stent in coronary IVUS.The Dice similarity coefficient ranged from 0.67 to 0.97, and the intersection over union for segmentation (including Jaccard similarity) ranged from 0.66 to 0.97, with the best performance for lumen and vessel segmentation and the poorest for stent and calcium.The sensitivity and specificity ranged from 62% to 90% and 88% to 99%, respectively, with the correlation to expert assessment generally above 0.9.Overall, the risk of bias was mainly related to patient selection (five out of eight studies) and the reference standard (three out of eight studies), and none of the studies was rated as having a high risk of bias.Due to between-study heterogeneity in the tasks, reference standards, and outcome measures, a meta-analysis was not performed, and the certainty of evidence was rated as low.The current evidence suggests that AI-based methods have good potential for analyzing coronary IVUS with acceptable accuracy, which could be helpful for high-throughput IVUS interpretation in clinical practice.They appear to perform best at segmenting lumen and vessel structures and worst at segmenting stent and calcium.However, due to the overall low certainty of evidence from these mostly retrospective studies, their use should be limited to complementing the work of experts in cardiovascular medicine.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Governance in Africa: Institutional Capacity, Regulation and Policy Implementation
items.abstract: In Africa, the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming part of the economic policy-making process, public administration, service delivery and technological development. Governments are preparing national AI strategies, creating institutional structures and joining in new continental and global governance efforts. The African Union's 2024 adoption of the Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy is an important milestone in the journey toward a coordinated African approach to AI governance (African Union [AU], 2024). But having a strategy or rules does not always mean it is implemented. This article explores the intersection of institutional capacity, regulation and policy implementation in the context of AI governance in Africa. The article presents the evidence from the recent African Union, OECD, UNESCO, World Bank and national AI institutions in Nigeria, and suggests that the reality of the problem is now more about implementation capacity than just about missing policies. African governments are constrained by complex challenges related to digital infrastructure, computing power, data management, technical skills, institutional coordination, finance and regulatory oversight. Infrastructure and compute challenges, lack of funding, and institutional coordination difficulties, as well as a shortage of AI-specific regulatory expertise, are all shared challenges across the countries (OECD, 2026). World Bank also states that connectivity, compute, data and skills are key prerequisites for meaningful AI adoption and governance (World Bank, 2025). The article concludes that the effective governance of AI in Africa demands to build the technical capacity of the public sector, create measurable mechanisms for implementation, foster inter-agency coordination, invest in building capacity to cooperate across the continent, and strengthen existing regulatory institutions. AI governance is thus more than a technology or regulatory matter; it is a governance challenge concerning state capacity and institutional effectiveness. In sum, this paper examines institutional capacity and regulation for AI governance in Africa, focusing on the specific issue of how to implement policy. This paper discusses institutional capacity and regulation for AI governance in Africa, particularly the question of the implementation of policy.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Electronic Design Automation: A Survey on Logic Synthesis and Netlist Optimization
items.abstract: Modern digital integrated circuits contain very large numbers of logic gates, and the conventional heuristics used in logic synthesis and netlist optimization struggle to explore the resulting design space efficiently. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have therefore been investigated as complementary tools for these tasks. This survey examines the role of AI in logic synthesis and netlist optimization, covering technology-independent restructuring of And-Inverter Graphs (AIGs), selection of synthesis flows, technology mapping, early prediction of power, performance, and area (PPA), generative hardware design, and verification. Related studies on reinforcement learning, graph neural networks, and generative models show how each technique supports a different stage of the synthesis flow. The survey also discusses the benefits of AI, including faster design exploration, improved multi-objective optimization, and early quality-of-results (QoR) estimation, together with remaining challenges involving training data, computational cost, tool integration, and formal verification. Overall, AI is best viewed as a complement to established synthesis tools rather than a replacement for them.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Diagnosis of Oral Potentially Malignant Disorders: A Critical Narrative Review of Diagnostic Validity, Prognostic Value and Translational Readiness
items.abstract: Oral potentially malignant disorders carry a variable but clinically meaningful risk of progression to oral squamous cell carcinoma, and their recognition depends on visual examination and on histological grading of epithelial dysplasia, both of which are subjective and unevenly available. Artificial intelligence has been proposed as a means of standardising detection, triaging lesions in settings without specialists, and estimating the risk of malignant transformation. This critical narrative review examines whether the published evidence supports these expectations. Peer-reviewed literature published between January 2000 and 27 July 2026 was identified through structured searches of biomedical and multidisciplinary scholarly indexes, supplemented by citation searching, and was appraised for study design, reference standard, validation strategy, calibration, reporting quality and clinical applicability. The synthesis is organised around five task families: photograph-based detection and classification, optical and cytological adjuncts augmented by machine learning, computational histopathology of oral epithelial dysplasia, multimodal risk prediction, and emerging large language and vision–language models. High discrimination is consistently reported for distinguishing lesions from normal mucosa, yet performance declines for clinically difficult distinctions, notably among white lesions, and falls further when images are acquired by untrained operators or originate from new centres. Evidence is dominated by retrospective, single-centre studies with curated images, histologically confirmed case mixes that differ from screening populations, and reference standards that inherit the poor reproducibility of dysplasia grading. The most methodologically mature work concerns whole-slide image analysis for predicting transformation, where externally validated models achieve discrimination comparable to, but not clearly better than, established grading systems. Pooled estimates from several meta-analyses are high but rest on heterogeneous and frequently optimistic primary data, and certainty is generally low. Prospective field validation, calibration reporting, decision-curve analysis and assessment of patient-relevant outcomes remain scarce. Artificial intelligence is best regarded at present as a promising decision-support adjunct for triage and research rather than a validated diagnostic replacement for clinical examination and biopsy. Progress will depend on multicentre prospective studies, harmonised reference standards, adherence to reporting guidelines for artificial intelligence and explicit attention to equity in the populations most affected.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Use and Learner Autonomy Among Secondary Students: The Roles of AI Literacy and Metacognitive Self-Regulation
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in secondary education has created new opportunities for personalized support, immediate feedback, problem-solving, and self-directed learning, while also raising concerns about students’ reliance on AI-generated information. This narrative literature review examined AI use and learner autonomy among secondary students, with particular attention to the roles of AI literacy and metacognitive self-regulation. Recent literature published primarily from 2021 to 2026 was identified, screened, and synthesized through narrative and reflexive thematic analysis. Across the reviewed studies, AI supported learner autonomy most clearly when students used it for exploration, feedback, problem-solving, and self-regulated learning rather than as a substitute for independent thinking. AI literacy helped students understand AI, evaluate generated information, recognize its limitations, and make responsible decisions about its use. Metacognitive self-regulation, in turn, supported students in planning, monitoring, and evaluating their learning while working with AI. The literature also pointed to challenges, including excessive reliance on AI, limited AI knowledge, inconsistent learner engagement, and differences in self-regulatory abilities. Overall, learner autonomy in AI-supported settings depends on how students use the technology and on the development of AI literacy and metacognitive self-regulation with appropriate teacher guidance. The study contributes primarily to Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by supporting responsible and learner-centered integration of AI in secondary education. From a sustainability perspective, strengthening students’ critical and self-regulatory competencies may promote more responsible, adaptable, and sustainable use of emerging digital technologies in education.

items.title: Artificial intelligence use, creative thinking disposition, and metacognitive awareness among EFL learners: a structural equation modelling approach
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in English as a foreign language (EFL) learning, yet its cognitive implications depend on how learners engage with it rather than on its use alone. This study examined the structural relationships among differentiated patterns of AI use, creative thinking disposition, and metacognitive awareness among undergraduate EFL learners. Using a quantitative cross-sectional correlational design, data were collected from 713 learners and analysed through structural equation modelling. AI use was conceptualised as cognitive-support use, creative-extension use, reproductive or substitutive use, and ethical and critical awareness. The findings indicate that the use of cognitive-support and creative-extension AI is positively associated with both creative thinking disposition and metacognitive awareness. In contrast, reproductive or substitutive use is negatively associated with these outcomes. Creative thinking disposition demonstrates a strong positive relationship with metacognitive awareness and mediates the effects of constructive AI use on regulatory awareness. Ethical and critical engagement with AI moderates these relationships, strengthening the positive associations between constructive AI use and both creative and metacognitive outcomes. The results clarify that the cognitive value of AI in EFL learning is shaped by learner agency, reflective judgement, and responsibility for meaning-making. The study advances a cognitively grounded account of AI-mediated EFL learning and provides empirical support for differentiating AI engagement patterns in both research and instructional design.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Theranostics: Integrating Machine Learning For Precision Diagnosis And Personalized Therapy
items.abstract: Theranostics links disease characterization with treatment selection and response assessment, creating a framework in which diagnostic information directly informs individualized therapy. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), deep learning, radiomics, radiogenomics, and multimodal data integration are expanding this concept from target verification toward quantitative prediction of diagnosis, prognosis, therapeutic response, dose, and toxicity. This review examines how AI can connect imaging, electronic health records, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, pharmacogenomics, and treatment response data across a unified theranostic workflow. Evidence from ophthalmology, dermatology, pathology, cardiology, oncology, drug response prediction, radiopharmaceutical therapy, and personalized dosing demonstrates that ML models can extract clinically useful patterns from complex datasets and support patient level stratification. In nuclear medicine, AI assisted segmentation, quantitative imaging, and dosimetry may shorten analysis time and facilitate patient-specific radiopharmaceutical therapy. In precision oncology, radiomics and radiogenomics can associate imaging phenotypes with molecular characteristics and treatment outcomes, while computational drug response models can prioritize therapies for molecularly defined disease. However, clinical translation remains constrained by dataset shift, limited external validation, data leakage, class imbalance, algorithmic bias, interpretability, privacy, interoperability, regulatory uncertainty, and insufficient prospective evidence. Future progress will require multicenter datasets, standardized data pipelines, transparent reporting, calibrated uncertainty, explainable models, federated or privacy preserving learning, prospective clinical trials, and continuous post deployment monitoring. AI driven theranostics is therefore best viewed as a decision support ecosystem in which computational prediction complements, rather than replaces, clinical expertise and experimentally validated treatment pathways.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-enabled value creation and competitive advantage in marketing: A dynamic capabilities perspective
items.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities contribute to marketing value creation and competitive advantage by integrating customer data, marketing intelligence, operational execution, and human strategic oversight. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design combined a survey of 300 marketing executives with qualitative evidence from three digital-first brand cases to examine AI maturity, predictive analytics, marketing integration, automation, and performance outcomes. Organizations with higher AI maturity reported 25.4% lower customer acquisition costs (CAC) than those with lower AI maturity, while Generative AI (GenAI) users reported a 40% reduction in content-production time. Qualitative evidence indicates that predictive customer intelligence can enable more anticipatory and personalized engagement, while human oversight, data governance, and authenticity remain important boundary conditions. Synthetic data offers a complementary option for privacy-conscious experimentation and model development. The AI-Marketing Value Creation Model conceptualizes competitive advantage as the coordinated conversion of customer data and AI capabilities into economic, operational, and experiential value through organizational processes and human judgment. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Marketing Intelligence, Marketing Operations, Competitive Advantage, Dynamic Capabilities.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-enabled value creation and competitive advantage in supply chain management: A dynamic capabilities perspective
items.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) creates strategic value in supply chain management (SCM) by integrating technological capabilities, organizational agility, and human expertise. Using a mixed-methods design, the study combines quantitative survey data from 250 global supply chain executives with three qualitative industry case studies to develop the Artificial Intelligence–Supply Chain Management (AI-SCM) Value Creation Framework, grounded in Dynamic Capabilities Theory. Organizations with higher AI maturity reported 31.5% higher demand-forecast accuracy and 14.5% lower logistics and freight costs. Qualitative evidence indicates that AI-enabled predictive analytics, adaptive decision-making, and operational integration can strengthen supply chain agility and resilience. AI can function as an embedded strategic capability when supported by organizational readiness, reliable data, and human expertise. However, these benefits are not unconditional. Environmental burdens associated with AI infrastructure and algorithmic management risks, including surveillance and reduced worker autonomy, require responsible governance and meaningful human oversight. AI-enabled value creation is therefore contingent on technological capability, organizational conditions, and responsible human-AI integration. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Supply Chain Management, Competitive Advantage, Dynamic Capabilities, Value Creation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence; Rethinking- Learning in an Era of HumanMade Technology and Capitalist Mechanism
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) have revolutionised the interaction between humans, knowledge and technology. What once needed years of formal education, years of institutional access or specialist's help is now obtained, translated, explained, reorganised in seconds. This unprecedented accessibility can help to minimize some of the age disadvantages in learning and provide lifelong education. Meanwhile, it asks the essential question: With the ready availability of answers, and analyses the decisions through own judgement, curiosity, critical understanding and intellectual independence. This paper critically discusses the overlaps between AI, Age, Education, Automation and Capitalism. But it's not necessarily the democratisation of education, it says, arguing that the democratisation of access to AI shouldn't be equated with the democratisation of education. While it can overturn the notion that technological skills are predominantly the purview of younger people, the potential for age disparities leading compounded differences in access to these tools, algorithmic bias, and confidence gaps and differences in digital and AI literacy. At the same time, the increasing machine-like nature of the educational activities threatening to change the purpose of education from learning and human development to efficiency, productivity and measurable outcome is awaited niche. Literature-based analysis is carried out by reference to the UNESCO, OECD, Stanford AI Index, IMF, ILO, and peer-reviewed scholarship along with the theoretical approaches of critical pedagogy, digital ageism and technological capitalism. Based on secondary data, the use of AI by students is already prevalent and evidence about the impacts on learning is mixed, and largely dependent on the context of use. This paper suggests neither technological rejection nor unconditional adoption. Rather, a human-centred approach should be pursued where AI is a tool for intellectual work and not an intellectual replacement in education systems. AI literacy, critical thinking, intergenerational learning, teacher agency, and transparent assessment and equitable access, therefore, should be central to modern education.

items.title: Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can contribute to the reasoning and communication represented in student work, complicating inferences from product quality to individual capability. This conceptual article develops an integrated framework for assessing cognitive ownership through mutual evaluation and outcome-aligned verification. Cognitive ownership is defined as a learner’s demonstrated capacity to understand, evaluate, adapt, and accept responsibility for consequential reasoning under specified conditions of assistance. Eight indicators are organized into four assessment domains: understanding, epistemic judgment, adaptive performance, and reflective accountability. Mutual evaluation combines independent student and instructor judgments, evidence-based comparison, and documented responses to disagreement; agreement is not treated as proof of learning. The framework distinguishes the quality of an AI-assisted product, capability demonstrated during assessment, and learning established through change and retention. A worked higher education example illustrates task design, scoring, and responses to conflicting evidence. Five propositions and a validation agenda address incremental predictive value, task sampling, feedback, fairness, and feasibility. The framework is proposed rather than empirically validated. Its contribution is to connect existing validity and evaluative judgment scholarship with a practical account of the evidence needed to support bounded claims about individual and assisted performance.

items.abstract: Introduction The widespread adoption of smartphones, tablets, laptops, and other digital devices has substantially increased visual demands among adolescents. Prolonged screen exposure has been associated with various ocular complaints, including digital eye strain, accommodative dysfunction, vergence abnormalities, and refractive changes. Teenagers are particularly vulnerable because of extensive use of digital devices for education, entertainment, and social communication. Continuous near work may place excessive stress on the accommodative and binocular vision systems, potentially affecting visual efficiency and ocular comfort. This study aimed to assess the influence of prolonged digital device use on binocular single vision parameters and refractive status among teenagers. Methods A comparative observational study was conducted among 201 emmetropic teenagers aged 13–19 years who had been using digital devices regularly for a minimum duration of six months. Participants were categorized into two groups based on daily screen exposure: high users (4 hours/day) and low users (4 hours/day). Comprehensive ophthalmic evaluation included assessment of near point of accommodation, accommodative facility, positive and negative relative accommodation, near point of convergence, fusional vergence ranges, stereopsis, and refractive status. A structured questionnaire was administered to record the duration of device use and associated visual symptoms. Results The study demonstrated significant differences in binocular vision performance between high and low digital device users. Teenagers with prolonged screen exposure exhibited significantly reduced accommodative amplitude, decreased accommodative facility, diminished positive fusional vergence, and a receded near point of convergence compared to low users (p0.05). High users also reported a greater prevalence of symptoms such as headaches, ocular fatigue, blurred near vision, eye strain, and difficulty maintaining visual concentration during near tasks. Discussion The findings suggest that prolonged digital device use may adversely affect accommodative and vergence functions, leading to reduced binocular visual efficiency and increased visual discomfort among teenagers. These results emphasize the importance of promoting healthy visual habits, including regular screen breaks, appropriate viewing distances, ergonomic device use, increased outdoor activities, and periodic eye examinations to preserve visual function and ocular health in the adolescent population. items.title: Authority, Typed Lineage, and Atomic Re-entry in Contract-Preserving Recalibration
items.abstract: Within Soft and Hard De-Attraction (SHDA), this paper separates the truth of operational objects from authority to act and specifies a quarantine, review and re-entry lifecycle for persistent-state artificial agents. Re-entry authority is conferred only at a linearizable commit that consumes the reservation and nonce; eligibility, reservation and approval states confer none. Given a suitable resolver, liabilities and failure history charged to semantic families survive aliases, merges, splits, epoch changes and rollback; restoration reapplies current ledgers, not historical authority. Under stated premises, Proposition G6 keeps confirmed, unresolved and reserved liabilities and actual consumption within every attributed cap, and Proposition G4 excludes, until revalidation, dependent authorizations after trusted recognition of a required invalidation and dependent effects after a durable receiver fence. Propositions G7 and G8 order leases, bound delegation chains but not aggregates, and bound hysteretic switching by score variation. An output contract fixes what each state and record licenses. Explicit-state studies close finite configurations, yield counterexamples for deliberate guard and ledger mutations, and retain overdue-duty and partial-effect states. In their timing models, local receiver checks cannot exclude stale effects before the fence without refusing valid work; atomic checks of the input's state (not the trusted log) and pre-fenced controlled changes exclude them by construction. The contribution is a typed authority interface over established transaction, capability, provenance and switching mechanisms, not production verification, liveness or measured superiority over a functioning runtime. Note on Version 2.0. This version replaces Version 1.0 (September 2026; about 9,000 words) and is a substantial revision (about 23,200 words). It states Propositions G4 and G6 to G8 under explicit premises (liability caps, dependent effects after invalidation, lease ordering and bounded delegation chains, hysteretic switching), adds an output contract fixing what each state and record licenses, and adds explicit-state studies with counterexamples for deliberate guard and ledger mutations and timing models for stale effects before a receiver fence. Files: the manuscript as PDF and a supplement archive (21 files) with the finite switching, authority, lineage and evidence-scope checks and the protocol witnesses; the full shared validation reports are in the supplement of the flagship record. The Version 1.0 file remains available in the previous version of this record. Publication role. Companion C develops the authority and re-entry branch of the Integrated Framework series on contract-preserving lower-to-upper recalibration (SHDA). Its interfaces connect Companion A's residual diagnosis, Companion B's disclosure and obligations, and the Technical Supplement's authoritative execution records; those items, the flagship and the technical working paper SHDA Algorithms for Scoped Evidence Reuse and Recalibration are archived separately. items.title: Automated Performance Evaluation and Due Process in Disciplinary Procedures
items.abstract: Digital technologies that are now increasingly being adopted in HRM have changed the way in which performance of employees is measured, monitored, evaluated, and managed. The systems for Automated Performance Evaluation (APE) make use of such technologies as rule-based scoring, key performance indicators (KPIs), machine learning, employee monitoring software, natural language processing (NLP), and Human Resource Information Systems (HRIS) for evaluating the behavior and performance of employees. While there is an array of advantages that the implementation of these technologies may bring, there are significant issues associated with the use of these technologies for disciplining. The score that is assigned by algorithms may have a bearing on any warning issued to the employee, development of performance improvement plan, suspension, promotion, termination, or any other decision affecting the employment. The study seeks to explore the link between automated performance evaluation and due process in workplace discipline proceedings. Concepts such as APE, algorithmic management, natural justice, and organizational justice will be developed. The study shall also explore technologies used in automatic evaluation of employee performances and how such technologies could be used in various phases of discipline processes. Special consideration shall be given to the right to notice, being given a chance to hear oneself, access to information/evidence, impartiality of decisions, explanations of algorithmic decisions, and the possibility of human review. Legal considerations include Indian labour laws and employment law principles, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 as well as the international approaches such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), EU Artificial Intelligence Act among others. The paper discusses some of the challenges associated with automated evaluation of employee performance such as opacity of algorithms, discrimination or bias, inaccuracies in the use of data, failure to take context into consideration, over monitoring, accountability issues, and power asymmetry. Finally, an automated evaluation process that is consistent with due process is developed.

items.title: Beyond AI Use: Examining The Predictive Quality of AI Dependency & Distress Intolerance in Avoidance Coping Among Young Adults in Mumbai
items.abstract: Abstract Background: As the reliance on AI keeps growing, it becomes important to understand its psychological implications. The study contributes to the growing literature on AI and mental health by investigating the predictive quality of AI dependency and distress tolerance in the use of avoidance coping in response to stressful situations. Aims: The present research aims to examine the predictive relationship between AI dependency, distress intolerance and avoidance coping among young adults in Mumbai. Method: 90 participants from Mumbai (60 Females, 29 Males) who were aged between 18-25 years (M=20.8, SD=2.38) and used AI apps like ChatGPT and Gemini, were selected using convenience sampling. All participants completed the Generative AI Dependency Scale (Goh et al., 2025), Distress Tolerance Scale (Simons & Gaher, 2005) and Ways of Coping Scale-Revised (Folkman & Lazarus, 1985). Correlation and simple linear regression was computed for statistical analysis. Results: Findings of the research indicate that AI dependency showed a significant positive correlation with avoidance coping (p < .01) and hence was a statistically significant predictor. Furthermore, distress intolerance showed a weak correlation with avoidance coping and was therefore not a statistically significant predictor (p > .05) of avoidance coping. Conclusion: The findings of this study highlight the predictive role of AI dependency in the use of avoidance coping when faced with stressful situations. The role of distress tolerance in avoidance coping needs to be studied further in a more diverse and larger population. The findings may help develop strategies that promote healthy coping skills in stressful situations in the era of increasing AI use.

items.title: Beyond Digital Government: Examining Indonesia's Readiness for Artificial Intelligence-Driven Public Sector Transformation
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze Indonesia's level of institutional readiness to support public-sector transformation through Artificial Intelligence (AI) using the Government AI Readiness Index. This study uses a descriptive quantitative approach, analyzing secondary data on the Index for Indonesia AI publication trends in the public sector, the global Government AI Readiness Index, and the Government AI Readiness Index for Indonesia for the 2021–2025 period. The results show that research on AI in the public sector has increased significantly in recent years, peaking at 195 publications in 2025. The United States, the United Kingdom, and China dominate the field, reflecting strong global interest in AI-driven government transformation. Globally, countries are assessed based on their Government AI Readiness scores. Higher scores indicate a stronger capacity in policy, governance, digital infrastructure, and AI adoption, providing a foundation for AI implementation in the public sector. Government AI Readiness: Indonesia's score increased from 58.14 in 2021 to 65.85 in 2024, then declined to 59.87 in 2025, indicating that the improvement in AI readiness has not been sustained. Indonesia performed relatively well on the AI dimension. Policy Capacity (77.00) and public sector adoption(73,77), but still weak at development and diffusion (44.09) and resilience (58.27). At the indicator level, Indonesia's strengths lie in e-government delivery, data quality, and policy vision, whereas compute capacity, AI sector maturity, and human capital become the main challenges.

items.title: Beyond the Black Box: Algorithmic Accountability and the Legal Regulation of Predictive Analytics and Machine Learning in India
items.abstract: The proliferation of predictive analytics and machine-learning systems has transformed decision-making across banking, insurance, healthcare, employment, policing, welfare administration, education and advertising in India. Algorithms no longer merely inform human choices; with increasing frequency they determine outcomes that affect individuals’ rights, livelihoods and opportunities. This transformation has produced what is commonly described as the “black box” problem: decisions are generated through processes that are technically complex, commercially proprietary and cognitively opaque, leaving affected persons unable to understand, contest or seek redress against them. Algorithmic systems trained on historical data further risk reproducing and amplifying existing patterns of discrimination against already disadvantaged groups. India’s existing legal architecture, anchored principally in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, offers meaningful safeguards for the processing of personal data but does not comprehensively regulate the algorithmic decisions that such data ultimately produces. Constitutional guarantees of equality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14 and of privacy, dignity and personal liberty under Article 21 supply an important normative foundation for extending accountability beyond data governance. This paper undertakes a doctrinal examination of algorithmic accountability in India through the interconnected lenses of privacy, equality, transparency, explainability, human oversight and effective remedy, and identifies significant regulatory gaps in the current framework. It concludes by proposing a rights-based, risk-sensitive and lifecycle-oriented framework for algorithmic accountability grounded in Indian constitutional principles rather than transplanted wholesale from foreign models.

items.title: Bridging the Human-AI preference gap: A persuasion-oriented tripartite framework
items.abstract: The remarkable performance of artificial intelligence (AI) systems on a wide variety of complex tasks has fueled its rapid adoption in recent years. Yet, many individuals still exhibit a human-AI preference gap, such that they prefer human-generated over AI-generated outputs and follow recommendations made by generative AI (GenAI) less than human advice. We conceptualize the rejection of a superior AI system in favor of an inferior human as a persuasion failure that necessitates psychological rather than technological resolution. Recent research has identified various interventions that compress the human-AI preference gap. We codify these interventions by introducing a persuasion-oriented tripartite framework that delineates three distinct paths by which the preference gap between humans and AI systems may be narrowed: (1) AI-centric interventions, which directly bolster perceptions and evaluations of AI systems; (2) human-centric interventions, which reduce the (often inflated) perceptions and evaluations of humans; and (3) hybrid interventions, which offer an integrated or reformulated alternative that combines human and AI elements. Ultimately, our tripartite framework illustrates how different persuasion tactics fundamentally reshape beliefs and attitudes about both AI and humans, thereby informing system design elements and communication strategies that can bridge the human-AI preference gap.

items.title: Characterising the ‘Genomics Friend’: Experiences of learning genomics in the workplace to inform implementation efforts
items.abstract: Large-scale genomic medicine implementation efforts are presenting relevant and authentic opportunities for the health workforce to learn genomics in the workplace, particularly from genomic expert colleagues or 'champions'. This paper presents novel insights on genomic experts' role and influence on learning genomics from the perspective of physicians not trained in genetics. As part of a study on workplace learning of genomics, longitudinal qualitative datasets were collected in 2021-2023 from ten non-genetics physicians working in hospitals in Victoria, Australia. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to characterise participants' perceptions of, and workplace interactions with, genomic experts. Deductive content analysis was then applied to sort and synthesise participants' relationships with genomics experts. Designated the 'Genomics Friend', these individuals are trained in genetics or recognised as same-specialty genomic champions and perceived as trusted and accessible sources of genomic expertise. Participants who had a Genomics Friend leveraged their established relationship on an ad hoc basis to address identified knowledge gaps. Sorting participants into the Genomics Friend Relationship Matrix demonstrated how having a Genomics Friend enhanced genomic workplace learning and practice for physicians across different career stages and specialties. These findings offer insights into how intra- and inter-disciplinary interactions and collegial relationships provide professional development opportunities through workplace learning. Moreover, we consider how genomic expert 'friends' could support implementation efforts by facilitating the health workforce to learn, adopt and practise genomics.

items.title: ChatGPT Use and Learning Motivation among Informatics Students: A Preliminary Correlational Study
items.abstract: Generative AI systems such as ChatGPT are increasingly used by university students for explanation, code inspection, idea generation, and immediate feedback. This preliminary cross-sectional study examines the association between ChatGPT use frequency and learning motivation among 17 Informatics Engineering students at Universitas Mulia, Balikpapan. Data were collected through an online questionnaire using a four-category measure of ChatGPT use frequency and four-point agreement responses for learning motivation. The original analysis reported a Pearson correlation of r = 0.685 with p = 0.002. Using the reported coefficient and sample size, the corresponding test statistic is t(15) = 3.642 and the Fisher-transformed 95% confidence interval is approximately 0.305-0.877, indicating a positive but imprecisely estimated association. The finding is consistent with literature suggesting that responsive AI tools may support engagement and perceived competence, but the correlational design does not establish that ChatGPT use increases motivation. Reverse causality, self-selection, prior achievement, digital confidence, purpose of use, and measurement limitations remain plausible explanations. The study contributes context-specific evidence from informatics students and identifies requirements for stronger follow-up research, including a larger sample, validated motivation measures, clearer characterization of AI use, rank-based sensitivity analysis, and longitudinal or quasi-experimental data.

items.title: Children, Robots, and Reproducibility: A review of recent reproducibility challenges in child-robot interaction
items.abstract: Given the rapid advancements and shifting requirements in the field of Child-Robot Interaction (CRI), it is crucial to understand how the field is evolving and if and how researchers are adhering to current best practices. We present a review of five years (2020-2024) of CRI research, under the lens of reproducibility. We analysed a total of 195 papers for transparency in reporting. We found deficiencies in reporting demographics (e.g., age of participants), study design and implementation (e.g. length of interactions), and open science practices (e.g., maintaining an active study repository). From our analysis, we identify a set of key challenges faced by CRI researchers and provide a checklist to systematically report CRI studies to help and guide research to improve reproducibility in CRI.

items.title: Comparing artificial intelligence versus human screening in systematic reviews
items.abstract: Systematic reviews are essential for informing health policy and practice. Artificial intelligence (AI) automates the article screening process and produces time savings, although the performance of AI screening compared to traditional human screening remains uncertain. We undertook this study to compare the performance of two agentic AI tools, namely Loon Lens TM and Catchii, to one another and to humans at the title and abstract screening level. We also compared Loon Lens to humans at the full-text screening level. We developed a de novo research question on the association between any of three ambient air pollutants – carbon monoxide, ozone, nitrogen dioxide – and the onset or worsening of Parkinson’s disease. A health sciences librarian developed the literature search strategy and we proceeded with human and AI screening. Screening results were compared using sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, concordance, kappa, and F1 score. We contrasted these statistics to those obtained by naïve guessing and regressed concordance (agree or disagree with the human reference standard) onto confidence scores provided by Loon Lens, which assigned a confidence level (‘Very High’, ‘High’, Medium’, or ‘Low’) to each of its screening decisions. Human screening was the reference standard against both AI tools; Catchii was the reference standard against Loon Lens. At title and abstract screening, Loon Lens outperformed Catchii when humans were the reference standard (Loon Lens versus human: sensitivity = 0.66, kappa = 0.74, F1 = 0.76; Catchii versus human: sensitivity = 0.49, kappa = 0.46, F1 = 0.50). At full-text screening, most disagreements centered around articles Loon Lens included and humans excluded. At both screening levels, higher confidence scores were associated with lower odds of disagreement between Loon Lens and human screeners. Given the panoply of available AI screening tools and their differential performance, plus the rapidly evolving nature of AI technology, researchers should pilot test their chosen tool at the start of each review. Sensitivity, kappa, and F1 are the optimal performance statistics to employ, especially at title and abstract screening, where the imbalance between proportions of included and excluded citations can inflate concordance and negative predictive value.

items.title: Comprehensive Ergonomics and Design Thinking for Occupational Fatigue and Risk Reduction in Commercial and Manufacturing SMEs: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: This project presents a systematic literature review titled “Comprehensive Ergonomics and Design Thinking for Occupational Fatigue and Risk Reduction in Commercial and Manufacturing SMEs: A Systematic Literature Review.” The study aims to identify, analyze, and synthesize the scientific evidence on the application of ergonomics and design thinking approaches to address occupational fatigue and reduce occupational risks in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in commercial and manufacturing contexts. The review focuses on examining the main approaches, interventions, methodologies, and findings reported in the scientific literature concerning ergonomics, occupational fatigue, workplace risks, human factors, and design thinking within SMEs. The study seeks to identify how these approaches have been applied to improve working conditions, reduce fatigue and occupational risks, and support safer and more effective work environments. The systematic review follows a structured and transparent literature-selection process. The initial search identified 983 records from the Scopus database. After removing 23 duplicate records, 960 records were screened. Following the screening and eligibility assessment stages, 40 scientific articles were ultimately included in the review. The selected studies will be analyzed using an evidence-based approach to identify relevant patterns, research trends, methodological characteristics, and key findings. The expected results include a comprehensive synthesis of the existing scientific evidence, identification of the main ergonomic and design thinking strategies reported in the literature, recognition of their contributions to occupational fatigue and risk reduction, and identification of research gaps that may guide future studies. The review is also expected to provide a structured knowledge base that can support researchers and practitioners interested in improving occupational health, safety, and workplace design in commercial and manufacturing SMEs. By documenting the search, screening, selection, and analysis processes, this project aims to promote methodological transparency, traceability, and reproducibility, providing readers with a clear overview of the evidence examined and the procedures followed throughout the systematic literature review.

items.title: Contract-Preserving Lower-to-Upper Recalibration in Hierarchical Agent Systems: An Integrated Framework
items.abstract: Soft and Hard De-Attraction (SHDA) specifies when verified lower-level recovery can support an upper-level revision without changing the external success contract. This condition is the framework's central axis, contract-preserving correctability: the joint condition, over separately judged coordinates, under which verified lower-level evidence may be admitted as the next correction and to which the system must return after each correction, containment, or revision. Because the components share budgets, strengthening one can break another; SHDA therefore organizes them as one closed loop along the axis, in which balance is an allocation of the shared budgets, not compensation. When a certified obligation fails, premise-level fault localization (T10) localizes the violation, within the recorded scope, to a false registered premise and its owner, a named record gap, or an unsound rule or checker; earliest failure sets diagnostic priority rather than establishing a causal mechanism. Under explicit assumptions, T1-T9 connect endogenous-error tracking, precision gates and probes, finite-phase progress, revision-aware certificate validity, transport between theorem epochs, repair costs, and same-episode outcomes. The scalar bounds and concentration tools are established ingredients; the proposed contribution is the integration layer: the objects, laws, and operations that exist only where the components meet. Three validation reports supply synthetic-loop tests (X3), planted-cause identification and fresh-audit repair comparisons (X2), and finite reachability checks (X1); their evidence is not interchangeable. In X2, certified full refresh matched budget-feasible diagnosis-guided repair in joint completion at nearly equal or lower cost, but a complete repair library and risk components with no failures observed in the retained runs left the repair value of diagnosis and risk untested; X1 separates post-fence compliance from safety under physical invalidation. The evidence supports scoped constructions and implementation obligations, not algorithmic superiority, deployed-agent safety, or unconditional convergence. Note on Version 2.0. This version replaces Version 1.0 (September 2026; about 9,200 words) and is a substantial revision (about 39,500 words). It organizes the framework around the contract-preserving correctability axis, adds premise-level fault localization (T10), states the conditional results as T1-T9, and adds three validation reports: finite reachability checks (X1), planted-cause identification and fresh-audit repair comparisons (X2) and synthetic-loop tests (X3). The Technical Supplement is revised as well (about 12,500 to 54,900 words). Files: the manuscript and the Technical Supplement as PDFs, and one supplement archive (132 files) with reproduction code, compact results and the validation reports. The Version 1.0 files remain available in the previous version of this record. Scope and status. This is the flagship of the Integrated Framework series on contract-preserving lower-to-upper recalibration (SHDA). The upload also contains the revised Technical Supplement, which states and proves T1-T9 and specifies the typed state, lineage, operations, attribution, disclosure and re-entry rules, the execution pipeline and the records. Companion A (residual genesis and dynamic feedback route attribution), Companion B (intervention-disclosure visibility and time-bounded selective nondisclosure), Companion C (family-scoped capability control, typed lineage and atomic re-entry) and the technical working paper SHDA Algorithms for Scoped Evidence Reuse and Recalibration are archived separately. The evidence consists of synthetic and finite-model checks; it does not establish deployed-agent safety or algorithmic superiority. AI use disclosure. Generative AI (GPT-6.0, OpenAI; Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) was used substantively in preparing this work, including source comparison, drafting and editing, and, where applicable, mathematical and counterexample checks and the writing and running of supplementary code. The research questions, framework and final claims were directed and reviewed by the author, who takes full responsibility for the content, including the accuracy of all references and reported numbers. Repository metadata were prepared with assistance from Claude (Anthropic).

items.title: Criteria for Assessing the Impact of Generative AI on Students' Dissertation Defences
items.abstract: This chapter explores the impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) on students’ oral discourse during the defence of Final Degree Projects (Trabajo Fin de Título or TFT, in Spanish). It addresses a significant gap in research by focusing on GAI’s influence on spoken language, particularly in academic contexts like dissertation defences. The chapter also aims to establish criteria for evaluating oral defences in Spanish universities, with a special focus on GAI’s role in their preparation. Based on a review of literature from Scopus and Dialnet, and a comparison of evaluation criteria across fifteen Spanish universities, the chapter proposes key indicatorsfor assessing these defences. It identifies six core competences for evaluation: communication skills, language use, structure and coherence, time management, use of visual aids, and handling questions. Also, it suggests specific GAI-related signs (e.g. impersonal language, repetitive sentences, or unclear use of sources) to detect AI-generated content that could affect the assessment of TFT. The chapter emphasises the importance of ethical GAI use in oral presentations and concludes with proposals for the responsible integration of this technology into education to help students and educators reach their full potential. items.title: Critiquing AI Surveys with a Case Study on Temporal Features for Trustworthy Computer Vision
items.abstract: A novel, thorough manual survey is presented, focusing on the trustworthy extraction and application of temporal features in drone video feeds for object detection and tracking. Trust stems from reducing the necessary scope of opaque, deep components, and externally accounting for hallucinations. This manual survey is used as a baseline for a first of its kind case study into the use of new end-to-end LLM based “Deep Research” tools for literature review purposes. It was found that such tools cannot currently be used to replace a manual survey on novel research topics, but may offer utility gauging method popularity.

items.abstract: This paper analyzes the requirements for developing Artificial Intelligence (AI) competencies among Vietnamese K-12 students by comparing three sources: (i) Directives from the Ministry of Education and Training’s Plan No. 1338/ KH-BGDĐT (dated February 6, 2026) regarding the 2026 National Conference on Educational Science; (ii) UNESCO’s AI Competency Framework for Students (2024), comprising 12 competencies across four dimensions and three proficiency levels; and (iii) Data on the education sector's digital transformation from the Ministry of Education and Training’s summary reports for the 2024– 2025 period. The comparative analysis reveals four primary gaps: (1) The absence of specific AI competency standards for learners; (2) Unequal distribution of infrastructure and digital learning resources; (3) A lack of systematic AI training for teachers; and (4) The absence of tools to measure students' AI competencies. Based on these findings, the paper proposes five key solutions and a threestage implementation model (2026–2029) at the provincial pilot scale, accompanied by a system of quantitative KPIs, specific measurement methods, and risk management strategies (detailed in the Appendix). Notably, the study introduces a validated process for establishing baseline data - a prerequisite for formulating, evaluating, and adjusting future policies on AI competency in K-12 education based on empirical evidence rather than intuition or anecdotal experience - thereby affirming the study's practical value and policy implications within the current context of educational digital transformation.

items.title: Death by a thousand papercuts: professionals’ imaginaries on ethicalization and technological determinism of AI in Sweden
items.abstract: Abstract While Sweden’s sociotechnical identity relies on a firm foundation of the welfare state and a frontrunner status, its artificial intelligence (AI) trajectory increasingly clashes with global market realities. Analyzing interviews with 13 professionals across the industrial, governmental, and security sectors, this article investigates the reconfiguration of competing Swedish sociotechnical imaginaries. Findings demonstrate a shift from an administrative welfare focus toward a security-driven enclosure. Navigating the friction between mundane “weak” regulations and speculative “strong” futures, practitioners engage in “strategic oscillation”, alternating between framing AI as an unstoppable, deterministic force and as a neutral, steerable tool. Within this evolving imaginary, “ethicalization” functions as a performative speech act engineered to establish normative legitimacy. By mapping the discursive mechanisms driving the European debate on digital sovereignty versus digital resilience, this article contributes to the broader empirical study of AI practitioners within sociotechnical frameworks. Specifically, it advances research on competing Nordic imaginaries by exposing the structural friction between geopolitical technological acceleration and the preservation of a high-trust welfare state.

items.title: Defining Computational Well-being Science: Foundations, Pipeline, and Agenda for an Emerging Field
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence, digital trace data, and computational modeling is reshaping how well-being can be measured, understood, and supported. Recent work has already proposed computational positive psychology (CPP) as an emerging direction for advancing positive psychology in the digital era. Building on this development, this article proposes "Computational Well-being Science" (CWS): a broader, theory-guided research direction that uses multimodal digital traces, computational modeling, and multi-source data to understand, measure, predict, and support human well-being across individual, relational, and population levels. I situate CWS within a "three turns" account of positive psychology's evolution--from institutionalization (1999-2010) through reflexive critique (2011-2020) to a computational turn (2021-present)--and define the concept through three foundations: conceptual, methodological, and infrastructural. I then distinguish CWS from eight adjacent fields, including CPP, and outline a four-stage research pipeline: datafication, modeling, interpretation, and intervention. Key challenges include privacy ethics, algorithmic bias, measurement validity, and the risk of theoretical hollowing. The central argument is that CWS should not be understood as a replacement for positive psychology or CPP, but as an extension of the study of human flourishing into a broader computational, data-intensive, and AI-mediated well-being science paradigm.

items.title: Dehumanized platform workers dehumanize customers: how algorithmic management reduces customer-oriented behavior
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how algorithmic management affects platform workers' customer-oriented behavior and to explore the potential mediating and moderating mechanisms underlying this relationship. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on social cognitive theory, this study proposes that algorithmic management serves as a contextual force that shapes workers' moral cognition and increases their tendency to dehumanize customers, which in turn reduces customer-oriented behavior. In addition, customer gratitude expressions may alleviate the relationship between algorithmic management and workers' dehumanization of customers. We collected data from a three-wave survey of 312 food delivery riders. Structural equation modeling was employed to test the proposed model. Findings Our findings suggest that algorithmic management is positively associated with workers' dehumanization of customers, whereas their dehumanization of customers is negatively associated with customer-oriented behavior. The dehumanization of customers plays a mediating role in this relationship. In addition, customer gratitude expressions weaken the positive association between algorithmic management and customer dehumanization. The moderated mediation results further indicate that this indirect effect is weaker when customer gratitude expressions are high. Originality/value This study clarifies the relationship between algorithmic management and customer-oriented behavior from the perspective of moral disengagement. By focusing on how customer gratitude expressions alleviate the negative effects of algorithmic management, this study further deepens the understanding of the moral function of gratitude expressions. In addition, our findings help advance understanding of workers' work experiences and offer practical guidance for improving algorithm design and enhancing service delivery.

items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence technologies into education creates new opportunities for individualized learning. In English lessons, AI tools can support the development of learners’ written and spoken communication, identify grammatical and lexical errors, and provide tailored feedback. This article analyzes the pedagogical potential of AI-assisted individualized feedback and proposes a six-stage model: Diagnosis – Analysis – Personalization – Feedback – Revision – Monitoring. The model goes beyond identifying errors by explaining possible causes, adapting recommendations to learners’ proficiency levels, and designing individual follow-up tasks. The article discusses the model’s benefits and potential challenges, the teacher’s role in supervision and pedagogical mediation, and principles of responsible AI use.

items.title: Developing a reporting guideline for the use of artificial intelligence in the conduct of systematic reviews: the PRISMA-AIM protocol
items.abstract: This protocol describes the planned development of PRISMA-AIM (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses–Artificial Intelligence as Method), a consensus-based reporting guideline for the use of artificial intelligence (AI) as a methodological tool in systematic reviews. PRISMA-AIM will be developed as an extension for use alongside PRISMA 2020. Its scope covers systematic reviews across disciplines in which machine-learning or generative AI outputs substantively inform review methods or content, including AI used directly, embedded within review platforms, or incorporated into agent-based workflows. items.title: Development and structural validation of the Artificial Intelligence Competency Scale for Nurse Educators (AI-CSNE): a three-domain measure of perceived AI competency
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare and nursing education has created new competency requirements for nurse educators. Despite this growing demand, there is a notable lack of rigorously developed and psychometrically validated instruments specifically designed to assess AI-related competencies among nursing faculty. This gap limits the ability to systematically evaluate nurse educators’ perceived preparedness for AI integration and hinders evidence-based curriculum development in nursing education. This study aimed to develop and psychometrically validate the Artificial Intelligence Competency Scale for Nurse Educators (AI-CSNE). A methodological cross-sectional study was conducted among 470 nurse educators from multiple nursing faculties in Egypt between mid-October 2025 and February 2026. The scale was developed based on the UNESCO Artificial Intelligence Competency Framework for Teachers and relevant literature. Content validity was established through expert evaluation and pilot testing. The total sample ( N = 470) was randomly divided into two independent subsamples. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was conducted using the first subsample ( n = 235) to identify the underlying factor structure, followed by confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using the second independent subsample ( n = 235) to validate the proposed measurement model. Internal consistency reliability was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha coefficients. Exploratory factor analysis supported a three-factor structure representing Foundational AI Knowledge and Instructional Application, Ethical and Human-Centered AI Use, and AI-Supported Professional Growth. Factor loadings ranged from 0.661 to 0.822, and the three factors explained 56.10% of total variance. Internal consistency reliability was satisfactory, with Cronbach’s alpha coefficients of 0.842 for Foundational AI Knowledge and Instructional Application, 0.810 for Ethical and Human-Centered AI Use, and 0.697 for AI-Supported Professional Growth in the EFA subsample, with comparable estimates in the CFA subsample. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the three-factor structure of the AI-CSNE, with excellent model fit (CFI = 0.989, TLI = 0.986, RMSEA = 0.023, SRMR = 0.046). The Foundational AI Knowledge and Instructional Application domain demonstrated the highest standardized factor loadings (ranging from 0.626 to 0.785), while the Ethical and Human-Centered AI Use domain showed comparatively lower but still acceptable loadings (0.570 to 0.734). The near-zero inter-domain correlations indicate that the three subscales are empirically distinct and should be interpreted separately. The AI-CSNE demonstrates initial evidence of structural validity and internal consistency as an instrument comprising three distinct subscales for assessing perceived AI competency among nurse educators. The near-zero inter-domain correlations indicate that the three subscales should be interpreted separately rather than combined into a single total score. As the scale measures perceived rather than objectively demonstrated competency, it is best suited for exploratory group-level needs assessment, research comparisons, program evaluation, and self-reflective development rather than for individual appraisal, certification, or high-stakes evaluation. Convergent, criterion, and known-groups validity were assessed and demonstrated no significant differences across subgroups, though further validation is required. The scale provides a foundation for research and self-reflective faculty development but should be used with appropriate caution until comprehensive validation is established. Not applicable.

items.title: Development of integrated supply chains and digitalization of agricultural product sales channels
items.abstract: The article provides a theoretical overview of the determinants of agri-food supply chain integration and develops a conceptual multi-level model for the digitalization of agricultural product sales channels. It shows that traditional linear distribution channels have exhausted their adaptive capacity amid geopolitical turbulence, climate risks, and rising transaction costs. To address the systemic exclusion of primary agricultural producers from value creation, the article proposes a transition to cyber-physical supply chains based on Industry 4.0 technologies. The article substantiates the economic impact of structural market disintermediation achieved through B2B agricultural exchanges, Short Food Supply Chain (SFSC) services, and logistics aggregators. The study outlines a synergistic technology stack: IoT sensors ensure continuous quality control and reduce physical raw material losses by 20–35%; blockchain and smart contracts optimize fund deposits via escrow, eliminating non-payment risk; and artificial intelligence algorithms enable predictive pricing and dynamic routing. The study finds that digitalizing sales channels reduces transaction costs by 15–25%, accelerates capital turnover by 4–8 times, cuts transport downtime by 40–50%, and increases selling prices for farmers by 7–15%. The paper focuses on Ukraine’s agricultural logistics under martial law, the redirection of export flows to Danube ports and western border crossings, and the role of the State Agrarian Registry (SAR) and the “eQueue” system in restoring export potential. A conceptual five-level model of the digital lifecycle of agricultural supply (“from field to settlement”) has been developed; this model minimizes the human factor, expands small businesses’ access to international markets, ensures transparent certification of grain batches, and lays the groundwork for the full integration of the domestic agricultural sector into the European Union’s single digital economic space. Keywords: agricultural logistics, supply chains, sales digitalization, Industry 4.0, smart contracts, blockchain, Internet of Things, B2B platforms.

items.title: Digital Barbarism and the Self-deregulation of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: In late 2026, the institutional landscape surrounding artificial intelligence reached a critical turning point as public warnings of existential risk intersected with major cybersecurity incidents, corporate resignations, and federal self-regulation frameworks. This paper evaluates the political economy of frontier AI governance by analyzing the rhetoric of "pacing" development and the voluntary "White House Accord on Super Intelligence" (Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities). I argue that corporate calls for safety pacing operate as an ideological mechanism that replaces democratic public oversight with closed, profit-driven corporate self-surveillance while shielding firms from legal liability. By framing technical software execution failures as evidence of autonomous superintelligence, tech elites legitimize market enclosure and top-down administrative control. Finally, the paper proposes democratic technoskepticism as an alternative framework that reclaims computing power, data infrastructure, and algorithmic knowledge as digital commons subject to direct democratic governance.

items.title: DIGITAL CAPABILITY, WORK REDESIGN, AND EFFICIENCY: A STUDY OF INDIAN MANUFACTURING FIRMS
items.abstract: Digital transformation is often described as a path to manufacturing efficiencies with the introduction of connected equipment, enterprise software and manufacturing data but fails to conceal that this is where the efficiencies are going. In this paper, we look at the management issue of making digital investments into the appropriate employee behaviours and integrated organizational processes. Suggests a combined effect of employee digital capability and work redesign is necessary to conclude whether the digital transformation can lead to increased efficiency in Indian manufacturing firm. Based on Indian empirical research, official data and work design theory, the paper proposes a capability–redesign–efficiency matrix and evaluates the extent of the evidence. Covered industries grew by 11.89% in gross value added (GVA) current prices in 2022–23 to 2023–24 and by 5.92% in employment. Additionally, the percentage of unincorporated non-agricultural establishments that used the internet increased from 26.7 per cent in 2023–24 to 39.4 per cent in 2025. Even if neither can be used to prove that digital transformation is an efficiency gain, combining both highlights the need for considering the evolution in production capacity alongside variable levels of digital uptake. Digital capability has more value when employees see and make sense of information, act on exceptions, and improve the process; work redesign provides them the decision rights, coordination procedures, and backstops to make them productive. Evaluation of the multilevel research design is designed for further testing with employees' responses and with observed plant results. The suggested gift is a more accurate description of how digital transformation can improve employee and/or organizational efficiency and when it cannot.

items.title: Effect of ChatGPT-Supported instruction on undergraduate students’ achievement in communication and media technology: Evidence from Northwest University, Kano, Nigeria
items.abstract: This study investigated the effects of AI-powered ChatGPT on academic achievement amongst 200-level undergraduate students enrolled in an Educational Technology course in Nigeria. The study also examined the interaction effects of gender on students' achievement. A quasi-experimental, pre-test, post-test control group design was employed, with a sample of One hundred and eighteen (118) students from Northwest University, Kano, who were registered for the Communication and Media Technology course. Two hypotheses were tested at the 0.05 significance level. Data collection instruments included the ChatGPT chatbot, a structured course outline with PowerPoint lectures, and the Communication and Media Technology Achievement Test (CMTAT). Data were analysed using ANCOVA. Results indicated a statistically significant effect of treatment on student achievement, but no significant effect of gender, although female students scored slightly higher than males students. Based on the findings, the adoption and utilisation of AI-powered ChatGPT is recommended to support and complement instruction across various undergraduate courses in Nigerian universities.
